bib.title: Chapter 3. Standard Practices for Text Generation with ChatGPT (Prompt Engineering for Generative AI)

question: Which simple, standard prompting techniques make LLM text output controllable, parseable and useful for common text tasks?

results.claim: Asking for a fixed number of items does not guarantee that length; code must validate the count or accept varying lengths.
results.setup: Hierarchical article-outline generation with GPT-4; illustrative, no measured rate
results.quote: For example, if you ask for 10 headings, you might receive only 8.
results.note: The 8-of-10 case is an illustration, not a measurement.

results.claim: JSON output commonly arrives wrapped in triple backticks (a json fence) and can be invalid, so the response needs parsing logic.
results.setup: Generating JSON with GPT-4; no frequency given
results.quote: Common errors that you’ll encounter when working with JSON involve invalid payloads, or the JSON being wrapped within triple backticks

results.claim: The chapter lists YAML advantages over JSON: no character escaping, readability, and comments.
results.setup: Prompt design for YAML responses with a No Items sentinel

results.claim: GPT-4 as judge of a simple conciseness rating matched the known concise/verbose labels in the example run.
results.setup: 10 answers to 'What is the meaning of life?' from gpt-3.5-turbo (alternating concise/verbose), rated 1/0 by gpt-4; printed output matches the style on all 10
results.note: Anecdotal single run; for complex ratings the authors say to evaluate the evaluator by counting false positives and negatives.

results.claim: LLM-based evaluation costs an order of magnitude less than human evaluation and finishes in minutes rather than days or weeks.
results.setup: Synthetic evaluation versus human rating; no data given
results.quote: typical-ly costs an order of magnitude less

results.claim: Majority vote over repeated classification calls reduces variance at the price of time and cost.
results.setup: gpt-4, same text classified 3 times as Compliment/Complaint/Neutral; expected output Neutral
results.quote: Let’s classify the same piece of text three times, and then take the majority vote

limits: No experiments: every example is a single GPT-3.5/GPT-4 transcript (2023-24 models) with no sample counts or rates.
Prompt and output text in the PDF is partly truncated mid-line (columns clipped), and several outputs are shortened with '...'.
The authors say evidence on LLMs as evaluators is mixed and that GPT-4 judging must be checked for reliability.
Warns a traditional ML classifier may beat an LLM depending on problem and training data.
The chapter's evaluator script sends the response as a second system message, as printed.
practices: Fix list size, format and commentary in the prompt and give an example list; the model otherwise chooses size and adds commentary (Generating Lists).
Do not assume item counts are met: validate the count or tolerate varying lengths (Hierarchical List Generation NOTE).
Prefer JSON or YAML over regex once structure gets nested (When to Avoid Using Regular Expressions).
For JSON, instruct: only return valid JSON, never include backtick symbols, response parsed with json.loads() (Generating JSON).
Give YAML prompts an explicit 'No Items' outcome and validate the parsed result with yaml.safe_load plus custom exceptions before passing downstream (YAML sections).
Allow the model to ask for more context by default with 'If you need more context, please specify what would help you to make a better decision.' (Ask for Context).
Unbundle a style into tone, length, vocabulary and structure and use it to guide new content (Text Style Unbundling).
Chunk long documents to fit context length, cut cost and keep summaries coherent; do not chunk short, simple or single-topic documents (Chunking Text).
Use overlapping sliding windows when semantic context matters more than minimising tokens or requests (Sliding Window Chunking).
Count tokens with tiktoken; max context length is input plus output tokens (Text Chunking with Tiktoken).
For sentiment, define labels, give an example per label and a one-word output format; handle mixed sentiment explicitly (Sentiment Analysis).
Use least-to-most chains and evaluate each answer before building on it (Least to Most).
Put the role in the system message for chat models (Role Prompting).
Answer only from supplied reference text, with an explicit refusal string, and ask for citations that can be string-matched (Avoiding Hallucinations with Reference).
Ask the model to solve first before judging a given answer; hide reasoning with an inner-monologue block the app strips (Thinking Time, Inner Monologue).
Self-eval: ask in the same chat whether the output missed anything and repeat until no refinement is offered (Self-Eval LLM Responses NOTE).
Use a stronger LLM to evaluate a weaker one, evaluate the evaluator with false-positive/negative test cases, and try programmatic checks such as response length first (Criteria Evaluation).
Majority vote of several classification calls reduces variance but multiplies API cost and latency (Majority Vote).

terms.definition: the process of breaking down large pieces of text into smaller, more manageable units or chunks
a technique used for dividing text data into overlapping chunks, or windows, based on a specified number of characters, tokens, or words
instructs the model to structure parts of the output that should be hidden from the user in a specific format
a technique that involves the creation of text prompts that, in turn, generate other text prompts
a technique that allows you to extract and isolate specific textual features from a given document, such as tone, length, vocabulary, and structure
a chain of prompts where each new prompt is based on the last answer
